newsitem.title: CANADA: Rogers sees no more significant sales.
newsitem.headline: Rogers sees no more significant sales.

text.p: Rogers Communications Inc vice-chairman Phil Lind said on Wednesday that the cash-strapped cable and telecommunications company does not expect any further significant asset sales.

"We certainly don't anticipate selling any further assets," Lind told Reuters in a telephone interview. He said some small sales may be in the offing in the medium-term but nothing of any significance.

Deals Rogers has reached recently will pour more than C$600 million in proceeds into its coffers. These asset sales include the sale of Rogers' 63-percent holding in Toronto Sun Publishing Corp, which it acquired in its acquisition of Maclean Hunter Ltd in 1994, to a management group.
A significant part of the total will come from the newly announced deal to sell some Ontario cable systems to Cogeco Cable Inc for roughly C$350 million.
Lind said the proceeds from the sales will be used to help offset the hefty cost of rebuilding Rogers Cablesystems' plant so that it is two-way and able to carry all types of traffic.
"The (cable television) industry has been going through a process of regional clustering and this continues the process, particularly for (Cogeco Cable)," Lind said.
"We have three Ontario regional clusters that make sense to us," he added. These include the fibre interconnected areas of Greater Toronto, the Guelph to London corridor and Ottawa.
The systems to be sold serve about 300,000 basic cable subscribers in Hamilton, Niagara Falls, St. Catharines, Sarnia, Wallaceburg, Peterborough, the Ottawa Valley, Cornwall and North Bay.
With the exception of Cornwall and part of Hamilton, these cable systems were acquired as part of the purchase of Maclean Hunter in 1994.
"(The sale of these systems) allows us to focus on our rebuilding efforts," Lind said. The proceeds from the systems sale will be plugged directly into the cable unit, he added.
Rogers president and chief executive Ted Rogers told the annual meeting in May that asset sales were a possibility as the company struggled to reduce the debt-level in the cable subsidiary.
